summary: Supply the age, the systolic blood pressure, the total cholesterol and the risk score and the Framingham risk calculator solves for blood pressure treatment?. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Framingham risk calculator work?
sections.html:
The Framingham risk calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports blood pressure treatment? in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex and the smoker); then you type in the age, the systolic blood pressure, the total cholesterol and the risk score (Result).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in years.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters of mercury. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as yes and no. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A number, expressed in pts.
  • A number, expressed in pts.

3 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Framingham risk calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Blood pressure treatment?=(25 ÷ 6) × risk score + (71 ÷ 6) × smoker × (age) − 605 ÷ 12 × smoker + (293 ÷ 24) × (the natural log of (age), 2) + (461 ÷ 24) × the natural log of (age) × the natural log of (total cholesterol) − 5201 ÷ 24 × the natural log of (age) + (91 ÷ 24) × the natural log of (HDL cholesterol) − 131 ÷ 24 × the natural log of (systolic blood pressure) − 667 ÷ 8 × the natural log of (total cholesterol) + 8615 ÷ 12
Blood pressure treatment?=(50 ÷ 7) × smoker × (age) − 218 ÷ 7 × smoker + (50 ÷ 21) × risk score + (253 ÷ 21) × the natural log of (age) × the natural log of (total cholesterol) − 1588 ÷ 21 × the natural log of (age) + (17 ÷ 6) × the natural log of (HDL cholesterol) − 85 ÷ 14 × the natural log of (systolic blood pressure) − 107 ÷ 2 × the natural log of (total cholesterol) + 14659 ÷ 42
Pmen=-(4701, the exponential of (risk score)) × (5000, -the exponential of (risk score)) + 1
Pwomen=1 − (100000, -the exponential of (risk score)) × (98767, the exponential of (risk score))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • Shown in milligrams per deciliter, and convertible to any of the 2 units on that chip.
  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • %, opening in percent
  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Framingham risk calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the age, the systolic blood pressure and the total cholesterol — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Framingham risk calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns blood pressure treatment?, derived from the age, the systolic blood pressure and the total cholesterol. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Framingham risk calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the systolic blood pressure, the total cholesterol and the risk score, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter systolic blood pressure in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Systolic blood pressure opens in millimeters of mercury and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Framingham risk calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
